extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in moral philosophy and self-reflection (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance-style personal essay reflecting on virtue, glory, presumption, and conduct; combines moral prescriptions, examples from history/myth, and practical reasoning aimed at guiding individual behaviour. The text advises inward conscience over public reputation and critiques ceremonies, vanity, and presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue for its own sake (conscience as sufficient reward)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue should be practised for the inward satisfaction of conscience and the regular ordering of the soul, not primarily for external glory or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay repeatedly asserts that 'the reward of a thing well done is to have done it,' and recommends valuing the internal testimony of conscience over public applause. Anti-patterns: doing good only for fame, seeking public approbation as the main motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do duty regardless of publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought to perform morally required actions even when they will be known to no one but oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Carneades' serpent—if you know someone is endangered, you should warn them even if the act will never be known. Anti-pattern: refraining from morally required action because it would remain private or bring no credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and fidelity beyond legal formality
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience can require refusing benefits that are legally obtained when they conflict with what one judges right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sextus Peduceus faithfully restoring a treasure entrusted to him; Cicero's reproach of Sextilius Rufus entering an inheritance against conscience though legal. Anti-pattern: using legal immunity or lack of witnesses as justification to profit from wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation is accidental and unreliable (fortune governs glory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public glory and reputation depend largely on fortune and chance rather than intrinsic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that fame is like a shadow; many brave acts go unnoticed and public esteem often precedes or outstrips merit. Practical implication: do not structure your life primarily to secure reputation. Examples include Caesar and Alexander whose renown owed much to fortune; ancient records are fragmentary and selective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inward steadiness (quiet life) to public renown
rubrics_metrics.description: Living quietly and in accordance with one's own reason and tranquility is a nobler aim than pursuing public renown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne values living 'in quiet' and advises seeking particular tranquillity rather than attempting to follow any common public recipe for it. Anti-pattern: sacrificing one's inner peace for the sake of gaining fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion (the multitude) is fickle and often ignorant
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgment of the crowd is inconstant, ignorant, and an unreliable guide for moral worth or decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make the life of a wise man depend on the judgment of fools; follow reason and let public approbation follow if it will. Examples/aphorisms from Cicero, Livy, Persius cited to underline this point. Anti-pattern: tailoring actions to please the crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act from duty, not for witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Courageous or virtuous acts retain their moral worth even when unobserved; one should not confine one's valor to those occasions where witnesses will report it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many brave deeds happen away from notice (between 'hedge and ditch'); conditioning action on visible witnesses reduces expected moral courage. Anti-pattern: only acting morally when observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony and externals can mask true character
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonial behaviour, salutations, and outward displays often substitute for genuine virtue and can produce hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes people obey ceremony (e.g., not naming body parts) while disobeying reason; cautions that ceremony can be used to appear humble while concealing pride. Anti-pattern: relying on ceremonial forms as proof of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not live for posterity or posterity's praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Expecting continued remembrance in history is vain; posterity is unreliable and ephemeral and should not be a primary motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne points out the fragility of historical memory and that countless brave people go unnamed; practical counsel is not to throw away present life for a few years of imagined future fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative/social uses of myth and ceremony (pragmatic falsehood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments and legislators historically employ myths, ceremonies, or false opinions to secure public order and encourage duty, which may have social utility despite being inauthentic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: founders such as Numa or Zoroaster attributed laws to gods to increase obedience; such practices are widespread. This is a descriptive standard about governance, not an ethical endorsement, though Montaigne notes its practical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish honour (public praise) from duty (private moral obligation)
rubrics_metrics.description: What customary opinion calls 'honest' or honourable is often mere public glory; one's duty may be independent and sometimes at odds with what is publicly praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice to women: do not mistake honour (public reputation) for duty; intentions and will (private conscience) matter more than outward appearance. Anti-pattern: excusing one's actions because they conform to public 'honour.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware presumption: accurate self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid an excessively good opinion of one's own worth; one should seek a truthful judgment of oneself and not be carried away by arrogance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne defends a balanced self-knowledge: do not underrate yourself unduly, but correct the soul's tendency to overvalue itself; presumption is the 'nursing mother' of many false opinions. Anti-pattern: pride, overconfidence, and self-flattery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undervaluing one's own possessions/qualities by fawning for the foreign
rubrics_metrics.description: People tend to overvalue foreign or absent things and undervalue what they actually possess; this is a form of vanity or misplaced esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne confesses he is prone to prize others' houses, horses, languages more than his own; practical counsel is to recognize and correct this bias. Anti-pattern: habitual preference for the exotic or external simply because it is not one's own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't equate outward show with inner courage (watch for counterfeit bravery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward signs of bravery or composure often conceal fear or cowardice; external display is an unreliable indicator of inner virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: soldiers who 'shift' in danger, counterfeit brave faces in the face of fear, or use the 'Platonic ring' metaphor to hide cowardice. Anti-pattern: trusting theatrical displays of courage as proof of moral strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value small, private virtuous acts as morally significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Modest, private acts of virtue (helping in small ways, risking oneself in minor occasions) are morally important even if they never achieve historical notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne emphasizes that many dangerous and brave acts occur in moments of little lustre and that conscience is a sufficient trumpet. Anti-pattern: only valuing grand, publicized heroic acts.
